2008: The Flood

She survived the road — the missed payment, the long legal walk, the empty rooms. Then the year itself fell on her street. Today the class watches one bad year become millions of empty houses, and millions of empty houses become an industry.

Our house: the 1972 house

Chapter 1 · From memory

No notes. Tell me the system.

Before the flood, the class rebuilds what it already owns — from memory alone. Last time we met the system that came for her: the servicer who held the problem, the national who covered the map, the crew who drove to the door. If the class can still lay that chain out in order, today has somewhere to stand. Because today, the chain gets tested by more houses than anyone built it for.

The system was built for a trickle. Nobody told it a flood was coming.

Say her name first

She was named once, in Class 1, and she is never named again. If this is a new group, or the name needs saying out loud to bring her back — here it is. Pick the name the class chose, or type it in.

That's her — the 1972 house. Same house, hardest year.
Say it in class

“Close your notes. Tell me the system, in order — who holds the problem first, who covers the map, who drives to the door. No peeking. Then I'll tell you what happened to that system in a single year.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Quick way back in. When a loan goes bad and a house falls empty, the servicer — the company that collects the payments and minds the loan — is left holding the problem. A servicer cannot hire its own crews in fifty states: fifty weathers, fifty rulebooks, thousands of towns no office can reach in a day. So the work is outsourced — handed to companies built to cover ground. Those are the nationals, firms that work across the whole country. The nationals hand the work down again, to regional companies and local crews — the people who actually drive to the house, change the lock, cut the grass, and take the photos. Servicer, national, crew. That chain is the system, and until 2008 it handled the empty houses of ordinary bad years without breaking a sweat.

How to run the recall, step by step

  1. Ask who is left holding the problem when a house falls empty. Take answers cold — no correcting yet.
  2. Push on the why, not just the list: “Why can't that company just hire its own crews everywhere?”
  3. If a hand is missing, don't lecture it back. Ask the question that leads there: “The national covers the map — but who actually drives to her door?”
  4. Close it in under eight minutes, standing at the chain, whole. Then say the sentence this class is built on: it was built for a trickle.

If you've done this work before

You work inside this chain every day, so say the part the newcomers can't see yet: the chain is not paperwork, it's capacity. Each hand exists because the pair of hands before it cannot be in fifty states at once. In an ordinary year that capacity is invisible — work arrives, work gets done. A flood year is when capacity becomes the whole story: the same chain, the same hands, and suddenly ten times the houses. Everything in this class — the growth, the deadlines, the stricter proof — is what a chain does when the trickle becomes a flood.

The line to remember: “The chain isn't bureaucracy. It's geography — and in 2008, geography flooded.”

The proof — where the chain comes from

This chain is the programme's own teaching summary of how the work travels, built up across the earlier classes: the servicer's fifty-states problem, outsourcing as the structural answer, and one carefully labelled example firm — Safeguard, bought and renamed in 1990 by Robert Klein, always taught as an example and never as the industry's founder. This class leans on that work rather than re-proving it. If a trainee asks “says who?”, the honest answer is the map itself — and the flood numbers arriving on Slide 5.

If this is all new to you

Houses have always fallen empty, one at a time — a job lost here, a divorce there, an illness somewhere else. In an ordinary year those houses arrive as a trickle: steady, spread out, one street at a time. A system built for a trickle doesn't need to be enormous; it needs to be reliable. What it does not need — until it suddenly does — is the ability to care for millions of houses at the same moment. Keep that picture: a good system, honestly built, sized for the weather it had always known. The next slides are about the weather changing.

How the trickle ran, step by step

  1. A loan went bad somewhere — one family, one street, one town.
  2. The road ran its course: help tried first, then foreclosure, then the empty house.
  3. The servicer handed the house down the chain; a crew secured it, kept it, proved it.
  4. The house sold, the file closed, and the system turned to the next one. Slow enough to check, small enough to know.

If you've done this work before

Here is the sentence worth saying out loud to a room that will inherit the flood's paperwork habits: almost everything strict in this industry today — the photo rules, the deadlines, the checklists — was either born or hardened in the flood years, when the trickle-sized habits stopped being enough. Trainees who grumble at the rules are usually grumbling at 2008 without knowing it. This class gives the rules their birthday.

The line to remember: “The rules have a birthday. Most of them were born in the flood.”

The proof — one number that shows the trickle

Hold the flood numbers for Slide 5; one quieter figure sets the scale of ordinary. In a normal recent year — 2024 — builders began 1,365,000 homes in total, neither boom nor collapse. The foreclosure road in such a year carries its sad, steady traffic. Nothing in that picture prepares a system for what the next three slides describe: a single autumn in which the banks themselves fell, and the road filled from end to end.

1,365,000Total housing starts, 2024 — a normal year, for scale
50 statesThe map the chain already had to cover — before the flood multiplied the houses on it
Chapter 2 · How the flood was made

The recipe was already cooking.

2008 did not arrive from nowhere. Back in Class 2, the class met the four ingredients of the 2005 wave: cheap money, loose lending, bundled risk, and belief. By 2008 every one of them had been cooking for years. This chapter opens the two ingredients a trainee most needs to understand cold — because they explain why so many of the loans were never going to survive.

A loan that should never have been made is a foreclosure that just hasn't happened yet.

Say it in class

“Nobody woke up in 2008 and invented a crisis. The recipe was already cooking — cheap money, loose lending, bundled risk, belief. Today we open the two ingredients that did the most damage.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Prime is the standard for a safe borrower: steady income, a good payment history, debts the borrower can actually carry. Subprime means below that standard — lending to borrowers who only just qualify, or don't, on paper-thin checks. In the loose years, the checks that used to stop a weak loan were waved through: income stated rather than proven, easy first years on the payment with the real payment arriving later, loans sized on the hope that prices would keep rising so the house could always be sold or refinanced. None of that is a family lying. It is a system deciding, loan after loan, that “good enough” was good enough. She was not in those loans — she is older, from 1972 — but millions of her younger neighbours were.

How a weak loan gets made, step by step

  1. A family wants a house; prices are climbing, and waiting feels like losing.
  2. The checks run light: income taken on trust, debts counted kindly.
  3. The payment is made to fit — easy first years, the real payment scheduled for later.
  4. The loan closes. Everyone is paid. The risk is now a date on a calendar, years away, in a future everyone assumes will be richer.

If you've done this work before

Connect this to the road the class already knows. A weak loan doesn't change the road — default, loss mitigation, foreclosure, auction, REO — it just guarantees vastly more travellers on it. And notice which loss-mitigation exits strain first when loans were made loosely: a modification can't fix a payment that was never affordable, and a short sale needs a buyer in a market where prices are falling. Loose lending doesn't just add volume. It quietly removes the exits.

The line to remember: “Loosen the checks and you don't create homeowners. You schedule foreclosures.”

The proof — the warning that came first

The programme taught this warning once already, in Class 1, and it belongs here too: in 1968, Section 235 pushed home ownership with subsidised rates as low as 1 percent — and by the end of 1973, 10 percent of those loans were in foreclosure. Ten in every hundred families lost their homes. Pushing ownership without careful lending does not create homeowners; it creates foreclosures. 2005's loose lending ran the same experiment at a far larger scale, without the subsidy and without the excuse of not knowing. (And keep the numbers apart, as always: 235 helped people buy; 236 helped builders rent.)

If this is all new to you

In Class 1 the class learned that a mortgage can become a bond: loans are bundled together and sold to investors, in slices, all over the world. That is securitisation. It is not wicked by itself — it brought oceans of money into housing and made loans cheaper. But watch what it does to care. The old local bank kept your loan for thirty years, so a bad loan was its problem, and it checked carefully. The new lender sold the loan on within weeks. If the loan went bad years later, the loss landed on an investor who had never seen the house, the street, or the family's paperwork. When the person making the loan no longer carries the risk of it going bad, making more loans feels safe — even when it isn't.

How the risk travels, step by step

  1. A lender makes a loan and collects its fees at the closing table.
  2. The loan is bundled with thousands of others and sold to investors as slices of the bundle.
  3. The lender's money comes back at once — free to make the next loan, and the next.
  4. Years later, when payments stop, the loss sits with distant investors — and the house sits with the servicer, who minds the loan for them.

If you've done this work before

This is why the servicer exists in the chain at all — someone has to mind loans whose owners are a crowd of investors who will never drive past the house. When a trainee asks why the client is a servicer and not “the bank that lent the money,” this slide is the answer: the lending and the owning were separated on purpose, long before the house fell empty. The chain the class recalled on Slide 1 begins here, in the bundle.

The line to remember: “When the risk leaves the building, the care leaves with it.”

The proof — carried, not re-proven

Securitisation is Class 1 material — “her mortgage travelled the world; she never moved” — and the four-ingredient recipe is Class 2's, where the average thirty-year rate in 2005 is carried at 5.87 percent: cheap enough that an ordinary payment could buy a big house. This class uses those settled pieces as its foundation and adds only the detonation. If the class is shaky on either piece, the honest move is back one class, not a faster retelling here.

Chapter 3 · The year itself

September 2008: the month the banks fell.

Every flood has a moment the water comes over the wall. For 2008 it was a single month. In September, the government took control of the two great housing organisations, one of America's oldest investment banks collapsed outright, and the world's largest insurer had to be rescued within days. The houses hadn't fallen. The money underneath them had.

She stood in her street the whole month, roof sound, walls straight — while the ground of money moved under every house in the country.

Say it in class

“Watch the dates. In one month: the two housing giants taken over, a 158-year-old bank gone, the biggest insurer rescued. The houses didn't fall in September 2008. The money did — and houses fall after money does.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Lehman Brothers was an investment bank founded in 1850 — older than the light bulb, a name that had survived civil war, depression, and world wars. It had loaded itself with the bundled housing risk from the last chapter: slices of bundles of loans that were now going bad together. On 15 September 2008 it filed for bankruptcy — the largest bankruptcy in American history — because no buyer and no rescue arrived in time. Bankruptcy is the legal admission that a company cannot pay what it owes. When Lehman fell, every bank on earth asked the same question at the same moment: who else is holding this risk, and can I trust anyone's paper today? Lending between banks froze. And frozen lending at the top becomes lost jobs, stopped building, and missed payments at the bottom — on streets like hers.

How one fall froze everything, step by step

  1. House prices fall; the bundled loans sour, all at once, everywhere at once.
  2. Nobody can tell which banks hold how much of the loss — so trust itself becomes the scarce thing.
  3. Lehman falls, unrescued. The question stops being “who is weak?” and becomes “who is next?”
  4. Banks stop lending to each other, then to businesses, then to families. Credit — the loop's third link — snaps at national scale.

If you've done this work before

Teach the distance honestly: Lehman never held her mortgage, and no trainee will ever work a Lehman file. Its place in this class is as the cleanest proof of the loop from Class 2 — jobs, rates, rules, building, all turning together, all capable of breaking together. When the top of the loop froze, the bottom of the loop — one family's payment — froze with it, millions of times over. That is the entire reason this industry has a “before the flood” and an “after the flood.”

The line to remember: “The houses didn't fall in September. The money did — and houses fall after money does.”

The proof — the month, dated

Here is the month as a matter of public record — four dates worth carrying exactly, because “the fall of 2008” is a season, but these are the days it happened on.

7 Sep 2008The government takes Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac into conservatorship — public control of the two organisations that stood behind much of America's home lending.
15 Sep 2008Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy — the largest in US history — and is not rescued.
16 Sep 2008The Federal Reserve lends $85 billion to rescue AIG, the giant insurer entangled in the same housing risk — one day after Lehman fell.
3 Oct 2008The rescue law (TARP) is signed, authorising $700 billion to stabilise the banking system.

Dates and figures as recorded in the public histories of the crisis — the conservatorship announcement, the bankruptcy filing, the Federal Reserve's AIG loan, and the statute itself. Teach the sequence, not just the month: rescue and collapse alternating, day by day, is what panic looks like from inside.

If this is all new to you

Two rescue words to own. Conservatorship is when the government steps in and runs an organisation itself, because letting it fall would take too much down with it — that is what happened to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac a week before Lehman. TARP — the Troubled Asset Relief Program — was the $700 billion authorisation signed on 3 October 2008 to stabilise the banks. Now the hard, important part: the rescues were aimed at the system — keeping money moving, keeping banks standing. They were not aimed, house by house, at the families already missing payments on streets like hers. The banks were steadied within months. The flood of empty houses ran for years. Both things are true, and the second one is why this class exists.

What was saved, and what wasn't, step by step

  1. Saved first: the payment system itself — banks able to lend, deposits safe, the loop's pipes unblocked.
  2. Saved second: the two housing giants, kept running under public control so home lending did not stop entirely.
  3. Not saved: the weak loans. No rescue could make an unaffordable payment affordable.
  4. Not saved: the families already on the road. For them, the road simply continued — into the flood years of the next chapters.

If you've done this work before

Hold the class back from the easy argument — “they saved the banks and not the people” is a slogan, not an analysis, and a good class deserves better. The sharper point is about order: a rescue of the system has to come first or there is no system left to help anyone through — and a rescue aimed at the system, by design, leaves the house-by-house work to the road: loss mitigation, the servicers, and ultimately the people in this room. The flood wasn't a failure to act. It was what acting at the top could not reach.

The line to remember: “The rescue steadied the banks in months. The flood ran for years. Her street lived in the second sentence.”

The proof — read the labels on the money

One discipline note, in the house style: $700 billion was the amount authorised — the ceiling Congress allowed — not the amount ultimately spent, and the $85 billion was the Federal Reserve's initial AIG loan. Authorised, spent, and lent are three different labels, and this class reads labels before it trusts numbers. Quote the authorisation as an authorisation and the lesson survives any fact-check; blur them and it doesn't.

Chapter 4 · The break, at national scale

Price fall plus payment shock — everywhere, at once.

Class 2 gave the class the break in one sentence: price fall plus payment shock equals default. 2008 is that sentence, spoken by a whole country in the same season. Prices fell, so the house was worth less than the loan. Payments shocked — jobs vanished, easy loan years ran out — so the family couldn't pay what was left. One break is a story. Millions of breaks at once is a flood.

She didn't need a storm. She needed her street's wages, and in 2008 the wages went first.

Say it in class

“You know this break — you drew it on the loop. Now put a country inside the drawing. Price fall plus payment shock, on every street, in the same season. That is not a family failing. That is a flood rising.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

When prices fall far enough, a house becomes worth less than the loan still owed on it. The industry word is underwater — or negative equity, equity being the part of the house the family truly owns. Picture it with hands: the loan is a bucket that stays the same size; the house's value is the water, and the water level dropped below the bucket's rim. Underwater changes every choice. Selling no longer clears the loan. Refinancing is refused — no lender swaps a loan for one bigger than the house. And a family that might have fought through a hard year on a house worth more than its debt looks at years of payments on a house worth less, and some of them hand back the keys. Even families who could pay sometimes stopped. That is why a price fall is never just a number on a chart.

How a house goes underwater, step by step

  1. The loan is made near the top of the market, on a price everyone believes will hold or rise.
  2. Prices fall — first slowly, then in a rush, as more houses come up for sale at once.
  3. The debt stays exactly where it was. Loans don't shrink when prices do.
  4. The gap between debt and value becomes the family's trap: can't sell clear, can't refinance, can't wait it out forever.

If you've done this work before

Underwater is the bridge between the money story and the property story this class serves. An underwater house is one market rumour away from the road — and the road's exits strain exactly here, because a short sale, the exit built for this trap, needs the lender to agree to accept less, in writing, while prices are still falling. When trainees later stand in a house asking “why did they just leave?”, underwater is very often the honest answer: the family didn't leave a home that failed them. They left a debt that no longer matched it.

The line to remember: “The loan stays. The value leaves. The family lives in the gap.”

The proof — the building collapse, counted

The price fall's twin is the building collapse, and this one the programme has counted exactly. In 2005 builders began 2,068,000 homes in total. In 2009 they began 554,000. Building didn't slow — it fell off a cliff, taking the loop's jobs link with it: every unbuilt house is wages never paid to carpenters, drivers, and sellers, and wages are the loop's first link. Read the two numbers slowly in class. The distance between them is the flood's engine room.

2,068,000Total housing starts, 2005 — the second wave at full height
554,000Total housing starts, 2009 — the trough. Building nearly stopped

If this is all new to you

A payment shock is any sudden jump between what a family must pay and what a family has. In the flood years it arrived three ways at once. The wage way: jobs disappeared — building stopped, then shops, then offices — and a mortgage payment sized for two paychecks met one, or none. The loan way: the easy first years of loose-era loans ran out and the real payment arrived, larger, exactly when money was tightest. The price way: underwater families who lost a wage had no exit left, because selling couldn't clear the debt. Any one shock, a strong family survives. The flood's cruelty was arithmetic: all three, same street, same season.

How the shocks stacked, step by step

  1. Prices fall — the house goes underwater; the exits narrow.
  2. Building stops — construction wages vanish first, then the wages of everyone who served the builders.
  3. Loose-era loans reset to their real payments — the bill grows as the income shrinks.
  4. The payment stops. Default — the first page of the road — multiplied by millions.

If you've done this work before

Say the human part plainly, because the room will do this work at real doors: behind almost every flood-era file is not a feckless borrower but a stacked shock — a family that could survive any one blow and was hit by three. The class doesn't need to excuse anyone. It needs to understand that volume this large is never a story about individual failure. It is a story about a loop breaking at every link simultaneously, which is precisely what made it a flood instead of a bad year.

The line to remember: “One shock is a hard year. Three shocks at once is a flood.”

The proof — the wage link, measured

Unemployment is the wage link with a number on it, and its public record is stark: the US unemployment rate reached 10.0 percent in October 2009 — one worker in ten, in the official count — the highest of the whole crisis era. Building's collapse fed it and it fed the defaults, around the loop, exactly as Class 2 drew it. One caution in the house style: 10.0 percent is the peak monthly figure, not an average for the year. Peaks and averages are different labels; quote this one as a peak.

10.0%US unemployment at its peak — October 2009 (peak month, not a yearly average)
Chapter 5 · Counting a flood honestly

The flood, by the numbers.

A flood this size gets told in numbers — and the numbers lie if read fast, exactly as Class 3 warned. Three counts, three different things counted. Read every label before you trust any figure, and the flood comes into focus: processes begun, properties touched, homes actually taken. They are not the same number wearing three coats.

Three different measures on one chart on purpose — the lesson is that they must never be swapped for one another. The fourth count, homes actually taken, is smaller than all of them and lives in the notes below.

Say it in class

“Three bars, three labels, three different things counted. The day you can say what each bar actually counts — without looking — the flood stops being a blur and becomes a map.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Walk the counts down from widest to narrowest. A filing is a paper step — a notice entering the system; about 2.9 million properties received one in 2010. A foreclosure start is a process actually begun; starts peaked at 2,139,005 in 2009. A repossession is a home actually taken — and its peak was a monthly figure: 102,134 in September 2010. Millions of filings became far fewer repossessions, because the road has exits and many families used them: they caught up, modified, sold. Quote a filing count as “homes taken” and you have multiplied the disaster — and misread the industry you're joining.

How the counts narrow, step by step

  1. A filing lands — the widest count, the most houses touched on paper.
  2. Some filings become starts; some families cure the loan or exit through loss mitigation first.
  3. Some starts reach auction; some are stopped, settled, or sold along the way.
  4. What remains is repossessions — the smallest count, and the only one that means a home changed hands.

If you've done this work before

This is the same discipline as the two peaks and the two piles, wearing its third costume — and it is the costume this industry wears to work. Volume forecasts, staffing plans, and fee arguments all get built on one of these counts, and the wrong one poisons everything downstream. When a headline number reaches your desk, the first professional act is not believing it or doubting it. It is asking what it counts.

The line to remember: “Count what the number counts — nothing else.”

The proof — the four counts, with their labels on

Every figure on this slide is carried from the programme's own Session 3 research, where the road is sourced step by step — the filing and starts series from ATTOM's foreclosure reporting, the repossession peak from the same record. They are repeated here with their labels intact, which is the whole point: lift any one of them out of this slide without its label and it becomes a small lie with a big number.

~2.9 millionProperties that received a foreclosure filing in 2010
2,139,005Foreclosure starts at their peak, 2009 — begun, not finished
102,134Repossessions in the single worst month — September 2010

If this is all new to you

In December 2010, about 2.2 million homes sat in the system at once. But say what the number is: it is two groups added together — homes in foreclosure (still on the road, still legally their families' until the road ends) plus homes already bank-owned (REO, at the road's end). Combined means added together. The programme's fact-check flags the classic swap in red: teach that 2.2 million as “REO alone” and you have doubled the bank-owned pile with houses the bank does not own yet — houses whose families were still fighting, still exiting, still home.

How to keep the piles apart, step by step

  1. Ask of any inventory number: is this one stage of the road, or several added together?
  2. If several — name them out loud. “In foreclosure plus REO” takes four extra words and saves the number.
  3. Never let a combined figure sit in a sentence built for a single pile.
  4. When in doubt, go back to the road: a house cannot be both on the road and at its end.

If you've done this work before

The stakes are not pedantic. An REO pile is work that exists now — houses to secure, keep, and sell. An in-foreclosure pile is work that may exist later, minus every exit every family takes. Staff and bid against the combined figure as if it were REO and you have promised crews for houses that will never arrive. The label is not decoration on the number. In this industry, the label is where the money hides.

The line to remember: “When a number is two things added together, say both things, every time.”

The proof — the figure and its fence

The combined inventory — in-foreclosure plus REO, about 2.2 million in December 2010 — is carried in the programme's Session 3 research with the warning printed on it, and it is repeated here with the same fence around it. That is how every borrowed number should travel: figure, label, and warning, as one indivisible parcel.

Chapter 6 · The flood at walking pace

Her street, in the flood.

Bring the flood down to one street — hers. In the flood years it was never just her house. The sign boards multiplied up and down the road. Lawns that had been mown for thirty years went shaggy in the same month. And each empty house made the next one harder to sell, cheaper to lose, and lonelier to keep — the flood fed on itself, street by street.

One empty house is a job. A street of them is a neighbourhood changing its mind about itself.

Say it in class

“Forget the millions for a minute. One street. Her sign board, then the neighbour's, then the one across the road. A flood is just a street where the empty houses started outnumbering the full ones.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The class already knows what vacancy does inside one house — the overgrown lawn signalling emptiness, water finding its way in, mould, then vandals and missing copper, until the house slides from lived-in to blighted: run-down, empty, and dragging its street down with it. Now multiply. A blighted house pulls at its neighbours' prices, because buyers price a street, not just a house. It pulls at their safety, because an unwatched house invites trouble to the whole block. And it pulls at their pride — people mow less carefully beside a lawn nobody mows at all. In the flood years this stopped being one house's sad story. Whole streets tipped, and once a street tips, each new empty house is easier to abandon than the last.

How a street tips, step by step

  1. One house falls empty and starts signalling it — lawn, mail, dark windows.
  2. Its price, when it finally sells cheap, becomes the comparison that lowers every neighbour's value.
  3. Lower values push the next family underwater; the next shock has no exit.
  4. Two empty houses become four. The street's story about itself changes — and stories move prices too.

If you've done this work before

This is the deepest honest answer to “why does the work matter?” that the course owns. Preservation is sold as protecting an asset, and it is — but at street scale it is also blight control: the mown lawn, the secured door, the house that does not announce its emptiness are what stand between one vacancy and a tipped street. In flood years that stopped being a nicety. It was the difference between a street that recovered and a street that didn't.

The line to remember: “Vacancy is damage. A street of vacancies is a neighbourhood deciding to give up — unless somebody is paid to care.”

An honest label on this chapter

The street-tipping story above is the programme's teaching account of how blight spreads — a pattern every experienced practitioner recognises, taught as a pattern. It is not a single study with a single figure behind it, and it shouldn't be repeated as one. What is counted sits on the slides around this one: the filings, the starts, the piles. Teach the pattern as a pattern and the numbers as numbers, and the class can defend every word of it.

If this is all new to you

Hold two pictures side by side. Picture one: a crew secures the only empty house on a street, in a quiet year, with time to do it carefully and a reviewer with time to check it. Picture two: the same crew, in the flood, with forty empty houses in the same county this week, every one of them decaying on the same clock. The jobs are identical. The work is not. At flood scale, everything has to be systematised: standard orders, standard photos, standard deadlines — because there is no time for anything to be improvised, and no slack for anything to be checked twice by hand. That is the world the trainees are being trained for. It was not designed in a calm moment. It was improvised under water, and then it hardened into the rules.

What scale changes, step by step

  1. Volume: one crew's week goes from a handful of houses to a route of them.
  2. Speed: vacancy damage runs on its own clock, so deadlines tighten from weeks to days.
  3. Proof: nobody can visit every house twice, so the photos must carry the whole truth the first time.
  4. Trust: with strangers checking strangers at distance, systems replace handshakes — portals, labels, checklists.

If you've done this work before

You already live inside this list — it is your Tuesday. The teaching point is the direction of travel: flood habits did not relax when the water fell. The deadlines, the photo discipline, the portal proof all stayed, because the system discovered under pressure that they worked, and because the next flood is a “when,” not an “if,” in every planner's private arithmetic. A trainee who understands that stops asking how to get around the rules and starts asking what the rules are for.

The line to remember: “At flood scale, the system is the skill. Anyone can care for one house; the flood needed people who could care for thousands the same way.”

The proof — the scale, in one comparison

Set the worst single month against an ordinary idea of “a lot of work.” In September 2010, repossessions — homes actually taken, the narrowest count — reached 102,134 in one month. That is the narrowest measure of the flood arriving at more than a hundred thousand doors in thirty days, each one needing a crew, a lock, a lawn, and proof. The chains from Slide 1 were about to be tested by exactly this. The next two chapters are what the test did to them.

Chapter 7 · The flood, stored

Two piles, not one number.

By the autumn of 2010 the flood's water stood stored in two great piles of bank-owned homes — one behind each of the two housing giants. Fannie Mae's pile peaked at 166,787 homes. Freddie Mac's peaked at 74,897. Two piles, two names, two numbers. The moment anyone adds them into one figure, they have invented a company that does not exist.

Every home in those piles was a street, a lawn, a lock, and a file — hers among them, or one exactly like her.

Say it in class

“Two piles, two names, two numbers — never one number. 166,787 behind one name, 74,897 behind the other. Add them and you're describing a company that never existed, holding houses that were never in one place.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are the two large housing organisations that hold and support home loans — the same two taken into conservatorship in September 2008. When loans they stood behind went all the way down the road, the houses landed in their piles: bank-owned homes — REO — held on their books until sold. In the third quarter of 2010, each pile reached its highest point: 166,787 homes behind Fannie's name, 74,897 behind Freddie's. These are agency inventory peaks — the most each organisation held at once. They belong to different organisations with different books, different streets, different files. That is the entire reason they are taught as two numbers and never one.

How a house joins a pile, step by step

  1. The loan goes bad and runs the road — help first, then foreclosure, then auction.
  2. At auction, no buyer tops the lender's credit bid — the bid of what it is owed.
  3. The house stays with the lender side of the table and, on these loans, is conveyed to the agency that stood behind the loan.
  4. It joins the pile: one more roof to secure, keep, prove, and eventually sell.

If you've done this work before

Piles this size are why the work became industrial. A pile of 166,787 houses is not a portfolio a person manages — it is a weather system a system manages: standard orders, standard allowables, portals, deadlines, audits. When a trainee wonders why a giant client's rulebook reads like a factory manual, the piles are the answer. Factories are what you build when the count passes what memory can hold.

The line to remember: “Two piles, two names, two numbers. Never one number.”

The proof — the peaks, with their quarter attached

Both peaks are third-quarter 2010 figures, carried in the programme's Session 4 research as the agency REO inventory peaks. Note the date discipline: a peak is a moment, not a year — say “peaked in the third quarter of 2010” and the figures stay true. Say “in 2010 they held…” and you've quietly stretched a moment into twelve months.

166,787Fannie Mae's bank-owned homes at their peak — Q3 2010
74,897Freddie Mac's bank-owned homes at their peak — Q3 2010

If this is all new to you

Four roles stand around every flooded house, and beginners blur them into one word — “the bank.” Keep them apart. Fannie and Freddie hold and support loans, and ended up holding the piles. FHA is different: it insures loans — it promises the lender it will cover the loss if the borrower fails — it does not hold piles of homes. A servicer is different again: it manages the loan day to day, collects payments, and holds the problem when things go bad. And a national is different again: it organises the work on the ground. Pile-holder, insurer, loan-minder, work-organiser. Four jobs. The flood makes sense only when the four stay separate in your head.

The four jobs, one house, step by step

  1. The insurer (on an insured loan) promised to cover the lender's loss — before anything went wrong.
  2. The pile-holder stood behind the loan's market, so loans could be made and sold at all.
  3. The servicer minded the loan monthly — and ran the road when payments stopped.
  4. The national organised the hands that secured, kept, and proved the empty house.

If you've done this work before

This separation is not academic — it is the map of who can tell you what. An order's rulebook comes from the client chain you're inside, not from whichever famous name stands behind the loan. Trainees who blur the players apply FHA habits to agency work and agency habits to servicer work, and the rejections teach them the difference at full price. Teach the four jobs here, kindly, for free.

The line to remember: “Piles, insurer, loan-minder, work-organiser — four jobs, never one blur.”

The proof — the roles are definitions, and definitions are checkable

Unlike the flood's counts, this drawer's content is definitional: what FHA insurance is, what a servicer does, what conservatorship put under public control in September 2008. Those definitions are carried consistently through the programme's Sessions 3 and 4 and match the agencies' own descriptions of their roles. Where this class asserts a number, it names its source; where it asserts a role, the role itself is the checkable fact.

Chapter 8 · Growth, under water

The flood made the industry.

Here is the turn this whole class exists for. The flood was a disaster for families and a catastrophe for streets — and it was also the making of the industry this class trains for. More empty houses meant more work. More work meant more companies, bigger companies, and a trade that suddenly mattered at a size it had never mattered before. The nationals grew with the flood, because the flood was made of their work.

Nobody in this industry celebrates the flood. But nobody in this industry would have a job at this scale without it, either. Hold both.

Say it in class

“The flood made the boom, and the boom made the system you're about to work inside. The nationals didn't cause the flood and they didn't just watch it — they grew with it, house by house, because somebody had to.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

A national is a firm that works across the whole country, not in one town — taking work from servicers and organising the regional companies and local crews who do it. Before the flood, nationals existed and did steady work. The flood changed their scale, not their idea. When empty houses arrive by the hundreds of thousands, a servicer needs partners who can absorb whole states of work at once, on deadline, with proof. Small firms that could grow, grew. New firms formed to take the overflow. Firms merged, built portals, hired vendor managers, wrote rulebooks. Other nationals followed the first ones. By the time the piles peaked in 2010, “property preservation” had become an industry with a name outsiders recognised — a thing a person could have as a career, and a thing a class like this one could be taught about.

How flood growth happened, step by step

  1. Volume exploded — the road delivered empty houses faster than existing capacity could absorb them.
  2. Servicers consolidated work with firms that could cover maps, not just towns.
  3. Those firms scaled: more vendors, more staff, systems to route and check the work.
  4. Scale became permanent — the portals, rulebooks, and roles built for the flood outlived it.

If you've done this work before

One labelled example, said the careful way, every time: Safeguard — a national firm bought and renamed in 1990 by Robert Klein. It is the programme's documented example of a firm that was standing in the right shape when the flood arrived — an example, not the founder of the industry. The industry was not founded by one company, and no single company should be taught as its beginning. And when you hear any company called “the largest,” treat that as company marketing — what a company says about itself — not as a verified fact. Marketing is what a company says about itself. Evidence is what someone else can check.

The line to remember: “The flood made the boom, and the boom made the system.”

The proof — growth, shown by the work itself

This chapter's claim is structural, and its evidence is the flood's own arithmetic from the slides before it: foreclosure starts peaking at 2,139,005 in 2009, repossessions peaking at 102,134 in a single month, and two agency piles holding a combined — carefully un-added — quarter of a million roofs at their 2010 peaks. Work of that volume does not pass through a trickle-sized trade unchanged. The programme teaches the growth as the flood's direct consequence, and the Safeguard label — bought and renamed in 1990, an example, not a founder — as its one documented, carefully fenced illustration.

If this is all new to you

Three habits hardened in the flood and never softened. Deadlines: when a county holds hundreds of decaying houses, “soon” stops being a date — orders carry due dates counted in days, and late work is failed work. Proof: no reviewer can revisit a thousand houses, so the photographs become the visit — before, during, after, labelled, checkable. Portals: paper and phone calls cannot route a flood, so the work moved into online systems where orders, photos, and invoices travel together and nothing counts until it is in the system. A trainee learning the trade today learns the flood's habits as simply “how the job is done.” This chapter exists so they know the habits have a history — and a reason.

How a habit hardens, step by step

  1. Pressure: volume makes the old, loose way fail in public, expensively.
  2. Improvisation: firms invent the tighter way under deadline, because they must.
  3. Standardisation: clients write the tighter way into rulebooks, so every vendor does it alike.
  4. Permanence: the flood recedes; the rulebook stays. The habit is now just “the job.”

If you've done this work before

Notice what this chapter quietly does for the rest of the course: it pre-answers the three questions every new trainee asks by week two — why is the deadline so tight, why so many photos, why must everything go through the portal. The honest answer to all three is the same sentence: because in the flood years, the loose version of each one failed at scale. Rules with reasons get followed. Rules without reasons get worked around. This class hands over the reasons.

The line to remember: “Every strict rule in this trade is a flood story that got written down.”

The proof — the proof itself changed, measurably

The programme's Session 4 tells the proof story in three objects: proof by mailed photograph (days of delay, gaps hidden until the envelope arrived), proof by handheld digital camera (faster, gaps hidden for hours), and proof in a portal (same-day, gaps visible at once, the missing shot demandable before the job counts as done). That evolution was already under way before 2008 — the flood is what made it universal and non-negotiable, because at flood volume the slow versions simply could not carry the checking load. Teach it as acceleration under pressure, not invention from nothing.

Chapter 9 · After the water

What the flood left behind.

Floods end. What they leave decides the next decade. The flood left tighter lending — the checks came back. It left a bigger attempt at help — the road's first exit, loss mitigation, written at national scale. And it left her: older now, on a street that had seen the worst of it, still standing. The industry the trainees are joining is the flood's longest-lasting leftover.

The water fell. The work stayed.

Say it in class

“Every flood leaves three things: new rules, new habits, and the houses. The checks came back. The help got bigger. And the houses — the houses are why you're in this room.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The class knows the road's first rule: help comes before punishment — loss mitigation first, foreclosure second. In February 2009, with the flood still rising, the federal government tried to run that rule at national scale: a programme (known by its initials, HAMP) that paid servicers to modify loans — rewriting terms to lower payments for families who could keep a reduced payment but not the original one. It was the modification exit from the road, industrialised. It genuinely kept some families in their homes. It also fell far short of the flood: paperwork drowned applicants, many who applied were refused or lost in process, and the foreclosures rolled on for years anyway. Teach both halves. A class that hears only “the government helped” or only “the government failed” has been handed a slogan, not a history.

How help-at-scale worked, step by step

  1. The family, behind on payments, applied through their servicer — paperwork, income proof, hardship shown.
  2. A trial period: months of reduced payments, paid on time, to prove the new payment could hold.
  3. If the trial held, the modification became permanent — new terms, lower payment, family stays.
  4. If any step failed — papers lost, trial missed, income judged short — the road resumed where it had paused.

If you've done this work before

The lasting lesson for this room is about occupancy humility: during the flood years, a house could look abandoned and be mid-modification, mid-trial, mid-appeal — a family still legally and actively fighting to stay. That is one root of the permission discipline the later classes drill: never assume a house's story from its lawn. The flood taught the industry, expensively and repeatedly, that the file and the house are different sources of truth, and the file must be checked first.

The line to remember: “Help first — even at national scale, even imperfectly. The order of the road never changed; only the volume did.”

An honest label on this drawer

The programme behind this class documents the road and the loss-mitigation exits in depth; the modification programme itself is taught here in outline — its launch in February 2009, its mechanism (paid incentives for servicer modifications), and its mixed record are the settled public history of the crisis years. What this drawer deliberately does not do is quote a precise count of families helped or refused: those counts vary by source and by what is being counted — applications, trials, permanents — and in this classroom, a number without an agreed label is a number left unsaid. The habit matters more than the figure.

If this is all new to you

The loop's third link — credit standards, the rules about who may borrow — swung from one extreme to the other inside a few years. Before the flood: checks waved through, income taken on trust. After it: income proven, debts counted strictly, paperwork deep enough that families with good wages and honest histories still found borrowing slow and heavily documented. Neither extreme is “natural.” Standards are a dial, turned by banks and governments, and the flood is the reason the dial sat at “strict” for so long. For this industry the consequence is quieter but real: fewer reckless loans means fewer guaranteed foreclosures — and a flow of work driven more by life's ordinary accidents than by scheduled disasters.

How the dial turned, step by step

  1. Loose era: checks light, volume high, risk scheduled into the future.
  2. The flood: the future arrives; the losses land on investors, agencies, and streets.
  3. The turn: lenders and regulators tighten together — proof of income, counted debts, documented everything.
  4. The long strict era: safer loans, slower approvals, and a work flow fed by ordinary misfortune rather than mass default.

If you've done this work before

Worth saying to a class that will mostly know the strict era as “normal”: the volume of preservation work in a strict era is not a sign the industry is dying — it is the industry at its honest size, serving the road's ordinary traffic. The flood years were the anomaly. A trainee who understands that reads slow months correctly: as weather, not as the end of the trade.

The line to remember: “Standards are a dial. The flood is why it stayed at strict for a generation.”

The proof — her own street, aged

One counted fact closes the chapter, and it is about the houses themselves. The median owner-occupied home — the middle home people own and live in — was 42 years old in 2024, up from 31 years old in 2005; about 47 percent of owner-occupied homes were built before 1980. The flood didn't just pass through America's housing; it froze it — building stopped, families stayed put, and the stock aged in place. Our house, born in 1972, is typical now, not exceptional: an old house with layered problems, in a country full of them. That ageing stock is the quiet guarantee that the work outlives the flood that industrialised it.

42 yearsMedian age of an owner-occupied home, 2024 — up from 31 in 2005
~47%Of owner-occupied homes built before 1980
Chapter 10 · Your turn

Read the label before you trust the number.

One habit carries this whole class: every flood number counts something specific, and the label is part of the number. In pairs, take each headline below and name what it actually counts. Then tap it to check your answer against the model.

Which count is it?

Tap a headline. Your pair's job: say out loud what the number counts — paper begun, process begun, homes taken, or two piles added together — before you look.

Say it in class

“No guessing the size — name the count. Filing, start, repossession, or combined. If you can label all four without looking, you can read any flood headline ever written, including the wrong ones.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The four labels, one last time, in the order the road produces them: a filing is a paper step entering the system. A start is a foreclosure process actually begun. A repossession is a home actually taken, at the road's end. A combined figure is two different stages added together — here, homes in foreclosure plus homes already bank-owned. Same flood, four counts, and the widest is nearly thirty times the worst single month of the narrowest. That gap is not an error. It is the road's exits, counted.

How to run it, step by step

  1. Pairs pick a headline and commit to a label out loud before tapping — no silent peeking.
  2. They tap to check, and read the model sentence aloud to each other.
  3. Walk the room. The mistake to listen for: any pair calling the filing count “homes taken.” Correct the label, praise the reasoning.
  4. Close by asking which count they would staff a company on — and why the repossession and piles figures, not the filings, carry that weight.

If you've done this work before

You've watched this exact confusion move real money — a forecast built on filings, a bid priced on a combined pile. The exercise is small on purpose: four labels, one habit, drilled until it's reflex. In the field the headlines arrive as client emails and portal banners, and nobody pauses them while you think. The reflex has to fire before the number does.

The line to remember: “Read the label before you trust the number — the label is where the money hides.”

The proof — the answer key, in one place

Filings: about 2.9 million properties received a filing in 2010. Starts: 2,139,005 at their 2009 peak. Repossessions: 102,134 in September 2010, the worst single month. Combined: about 2.2 million in December 2010, in foreclosure plus REO together — never REO alone. All four carried from the programme's Session 3 research with labels intact, as they appear on Slide 5.

Chapter 11 · The close

She is still standing.

End where the class began: at her door. She went through the flood the way she went through everything — standing in her street while the money weather changed around her. The banks fell and were rescued. The piles rose and slowly drained. The industry grew up around her in a handful of years. And the work — the securing, the keeping, the proving — turned out to be permanent.

Next, the class steps back and gathers the other major things — the rest of the story this flood sits inside — before it walks the full work circle, order to payment, and finally takes up the work itself.

Say it in class

“The flood was never really about banks. It was about millions of her — one house, one street, one file at a time. The system grew because somebody had to care for all of them at once. That somebody, from the next classes on, is you.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The whole class in four breaths. The recipe: cheap money, loose lending, bundled risk, and belief cooked for years before anyone said the word crisis. The month: September 2008 — the giants taken over, Lehman fallen, the insurer rescued, the rescue law signed — the money broke before the houses did. The labels: filings, starts, repossessions, and combined piles are different counts, and reading the label is a professional skill, not a pedant's hobby. The industry: the flood of empty houses grew the nationals, hardened the deadlines and the proof, and left a permanent trade — the one being taught in this room.

The flood, in one telling, step by step

  1. The recipe cooked: loans made loosely, risk bundled away, prices believed immortal.
  2. Prices fell; houses went underwater; jobs vanished; payments shocked — the loop broke everywhere at once.
  3. September 2008: the money system itself fell, was partly rescued, and steadied — while the road filled for years.
  4. The counts peaked in their order: starts in 2009, filings and the two piles in 2010 — each label saying exactly what it counts.
  5. The work industrialised: nationals grew, proof tightened, portals took over — and the industry stayed.

If you've done this work before

Close the class on proportion. The flood is the industry's founding weather, but it is not the industry's daily weather — the daily weather is ordinary: a lost job, a divorce, an illness, one house on one street. A trainee who can hold both scales at once — millions then, one careful job now — has the judgement this trade actually runs on. Everything after this class is craft: the other major things, the full work circle, and then the work itself, done properly, house by house.

The line to remember: “Millions then. One house now. Same road, same care.”

The proof — the class, auditable in one glance

Every load-bearing figure in this class, gathered: foreclosure starts peaked at 2,139,005 in 2009; about 2.9 million properties received a filing in 2010; repossessions peaked at 102,134 in September 2010; the combined in-foreclosure plus REO inventory stood at about 2.2 million in December 2010; Fannie Mae's REO pile peaked at 166,787 and Freddie Mac's at 74,897, both in Q3 2010; total starts fell from 2,068,000 in 2005 to 554,000 in 2009; unemployment peaked at 10.0 percent in October 2009; and the September 2008 dates — 7th, 15th, 16th, and 3 October — stand as public record. Nothing else in the class needs a number, and no number in the class travels without its label.

The logic behind this page

Why the 2008 demo is built the way it is, where it stands in the sequence, and what its numbers do — and don't — claim. One teacher to another, before the class walks in.

Where this page stands

This demo follows the Safeguard demo in the build order the teacher set: Class 1 (her rise), Class 2 (the peaks and the loop), the Safeguard demo (the system that came for her), and now 2008 — the flood that tested that system past anything it was built for. It deliberately leans on the earlier pages instead of repeating them: the road and its labels are Class 3's material, the system and the Safeguard label are the previous demo's, and the recipe and the loop are Class 2's. What this page adds is the year itself — the detonation, the honest counting of the flood, and the industry's growth — taught as one story, in the same house and the same voice.

Why the numbers carry fences

  • Every figure travels with its label. Filings, starts, repossessions, and combined inventory are four different counts; the page never lets one stand in for another, because that swap is the single most common way the flood gets mis-taught.
  • The two piles are never added. 166,787 and 74,897 belong to different organisations; a summed figure would describe a company that does not exist.
  • Authorised is not spent, a peak is not an average. The $700 billion TARP figure is taught as an authorisation, and the 10.0 percent unemployment figure as a peak month — labels the page states out loud rather than assuming.
  • What isn't counted is labelled as pattern. The street-tipping account and the modification programme's mixed record are taught as patterns and outlines, with the honesty boxes saying so — the class never has to guess which sentences are statistics and which are teaching illustrations.

Sources this page stands on

  • The programme's own blueprint and Session 3–4 research: the road and its labels, the filing/start/repossession counts (ATTOM foreclosure reporting as carried there), the combined December 2010 inventory, the two agency REO peaks (Q3 2010), the housing-starts series (2,068,000 in 2005; 554,000 in 2009; 1,365,000 in 2024), the median home-age figures, and the Safeguard label (bought and renamed 1990 by Robert Klein — an example, never the founder).
  • Public record of the crisis: the conservatorship of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (7 September 2008), the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy filing (15 September 2008), the Federal Reserve's initial $85 billion AIG loan (16 September 2008), the TARP authorisation of $700 billion (signed 3 October 2008), and the unemployment peak of 10.0 percent (October 2009, Bureau of Labor Statistics).
  • No real client, company, work-order, or property data appears anywhere in this demo. The house is a fictional composite, and the firm named is a documented historical example, labelled as such every time it appears.

2008 Demo — “2008: The Flood.” A teaching demo in the same sequence as Class 1, Class 2, and the Safeguard demo: same house, same voice. The house is a fictional composite; every number is carried with its label from the programme's research or the public record, as noted on the logic page.
